axes.label: Craft & polish
axes.description: Visual quality, typography, colour, composition, motion feel, finish. Would a discerning person believe a human designed this on purpose?

axes.label: Technical ambition
axes.description: How hard is what was actually built, and is it built correctly? Real technique versus the cheapest thing that looks similar.

axes.label: Brief adherence
axes.description: Did it do everything the prompt asked, completely, including the output contract? Stubs and TODOs count against.

axes.label: Originality
axes.description: Is the idea and its execution distinctive, or is it the median AI answer to this prompt?

`matType` is effectively dead: it is assigned by float equality against `core`/`ribbon` after two `smin` blends, so it almost never resolves truthfully and the per-material shading branch (`hitMat * 0.3`) barely varies.

The hint reads 'Drag to distort topological field', but the drag state is written into `u_mouse.z` and never read anywhere in the fragment shader — dragging is identical to hovering. The UI promises an interaction the shader does not implement.
'Cauchy chromatic dispersion' is three `map()` density probes along refracted directions fed through smoothstep, not refraction — a legitimate cheap approximation, but the naming oversells it.

The shader is labelled and presented as a 'volumetric SDF,' but the volume effect is only an in-loop inverse-distance glow accumulation around an SDF surface, not a physically meaningful volumetric medium.

Material assignment relies on exact floating-point equality after smooth-min composition (`d == core` / `d == ribbon`), so those material distinctions are unreliable and usually collapse to the cage material.

Shader compilation/link failures are caught for fallback display, but are also explicitly sent to `console.error`, which would violate the no-console-errors output constraint in a shader-failure case.
